newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Several wounded by gunfire at Albania poll rally.
newsitem.headline: Several wounded by gunfire at Albania poll rally.

text.p: Several people have been wounded by gunfire during a rally held by Albanian President Sali Berisha as an upsurge of violence hit the Balkan state three days before a general election.

Foreign journalists who attended Thursday's rally in Lushnje, about 80 km (50 miles) south of the capital Tirana, said shooting broke out near the town hall where Berisha was addressing a crowd of several hundred.
One journalist said she saw at least eight people with injuries in the town hospital.

Fresh violence between rival gangs has also erupted in the past few days in the Adriatic port of Vlore, focal point of a rebellion sparked earlier this year by the collapse of shady investment schemes in which many Albanians had invested. About 1,500 people have been killed since the rebellion broke out.
Troops of the 7,000-strong multinational force dispatched to Albania last month restored order in Vlore on Thursday by moving through the town with armoured vehicles.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation on Europe (OSCE) is supervising Sunday's snap election. Hundreds of international observers were due to travel across the country on Friday to prepare to monitor the voting.

Berisha is not seeking re-election. But he has been campaigning hard to retain the big majority his Democratic Party won last year against a challenge by the Socialists, reformed heirs to Albania's former ruling hardline Communist Party.

In Lushnje, journalists said gunfire was heard at a distance behind the crowd five minutes after the president began his address. The president's bodyguards returned fire but it was not clear how the people were wounded.
Berisha left Lushnje and went on to other rallies in the town of Kavaje and the port of Durres.
Both Berisha's Democrats and the Socialists under economist Fatos Nano have scheduled rallies in Tirana's Skanderbeg Square at different times on Friday, the final day of campaigning.
The election is seen by the international community as the only way to restore stability in Albania.
The OSCE's special envoy, former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky, told the Albanian people on Thursday that every effort would be made to ensure the vote passed off smoothly.
"The election on Sunday will be one of the most important political decisions that the Albanian people have to take," Vranitzky said in a live television interview in English.
"We will take care that the election can be held and dangers that might be in the hearts or minds of the people will be minimised as best as we can."

Vranitzky said he was confident it would be agreed to close polling stations earlier than planned -- and well before nightfall -- to help ensure the safety of voters and observers. A final decision is in the hands of the Constitutional Court.
Berisha agreed at the height of the rebellion in March to hold the election and to appoint an interim multi-party government, headed by a Socialist.
The darling of the West in the early 1990s, Berisha's support from abroad faded after observers denounced last year's parliamentary election as unfair.
It ebbed still further when he proclaimed a state of emergency on March 2 as the rebellion sharply worsened and he engineered his re-election by parliament the next day.
Campaigning has been at best sporadic, with both the Democrats and Socialists unable to hold rallies in areas dominated by rival supporters or outside government control.
Predicting the outcome of the vote is nearly impossible, but both leading parties have said they will win.
